title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 14: The Death Penalty Cases -- More of the Same
primary_topics: Chapter 14 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's survey of death-penalty jurisprudence during his sixth year (October 2000-October 2001), continuing the 'philosophical and juridical opposition' to the death penalty he developed in his earlier books, with the chapter's title ('More of the Same') signaling the continuity of doctrine and of his dissent

The de facto no-execution policy: President Estrada's Jubilee-Year moratorium (announced March 25, 2000) continued by the Arroyo government (Sec. Perez, March 7, 2001; Exec. Sec. de Villa, April 7, 2001 -- 'no executions... during [Arroyo's] three-year term'), so no one had been executed since March 25, 2000, even as repeal bills were filed and the Court kept reviewing death sentences

The qualifying-circumstances doctrine and a numbered catalogue of jurisprudential developments: special qualifying circumstances under Section 11 of RA 7659 must be BOTH alleged in the information AND proven (e.g., minority, relationship, use of a deadly weapon), so frequent trial-court lapses led the Court to reduce many death sentences to reclusion perpetua; plus People v. Catubig (exemplary damages on the civil side even when an aggravating circumstance is unalleged) and People v. Gonzales (treachery not lightly inferred)

The improvident-plea line of cases (Aranzado, Sta. Teresa, Chua) enforcing the 'searching inquiry' required by Rule 116, Section 3 and chastising 'lackluster' defense counsel; and Justice Vitug's argument that a mandatory single death penalty is an unconstitutional legislative infringement on judicial prerogative, supported by US precedents and the worldwide abolition trend
sub_topics: CJP's standing opposition to the Death Penalty Law (RA 7659) and lethal injection (RA 8177), documented in 'Battles in the Supreme Court,' 'Leadership by Example' and 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity'

The no-execution policy: Estrada's 11-month Jubilee moratorium (March 25, 2000) and the Arroyo government's continuation through automatic commutation -- 'no executions of death row convicts during [Arroyo's] three-year term'; no one placed in the lethal-injection chamber since March 25, 2000

Pending repeal bills filed by Senators Aquilino Pimentel Jr. and John Osmena and Representatives Krisel Lagman-Luistro and Emilio Macias II; the Court continues reviewing death sentences because the law was not repealed

The qualifying-circumstances rule: under Section 11 of RA 7659, special qualifying circumstances must be both alleged in the information and proven at trial; many RTCs failed this, so the Court reduced numerous death sentences (e.g., failure to allege 'use of deadly weapon,' minority not independently proven, 'cousins-in-law' not a qualifying relationship, victim calling the appellant 'Lolo' insufficient)

People v. Catubig (per Vitug): exemplary or corrective damages may be awarded on the CIVIL side when an aggravating circumstance -- ordinary or qualifying -- is proven, even if the offense predated the December 1, 2000 Revised Rules requiring such circumstances to be alleged, since procedural rules cannot impair the victim's vested civil rights

People v. Gonzales (per Gonzaga-Reyes): treachery cannot be inferred merely because a defenseless woman (Feliber Andres) was killed near Loyola Memorial Park by a shot 'not aiming at anybody in particular'; the crime was homicide -- over the dissent of Justice Pardo (joined by Puno, Kapunan and CJP), who found treachery and aberratio ictus and would have convicted of murder

The improvident-plea cases and the Rule 116, Section 3 'searching inquiry': in People v. Aranzado (per Davide, CJ) the Court detailed the required inquiry (how the accused came into custody, whether assisted by competent counsel, personality profile, the exact penalty, narration of the incident) and chastised both the trial court's defective inquiry and counsel Atty. Balo's 'lackadaisical' performance

CJP's own ponencia in People v. Sta. Teresa, stressing the mandatory three-step duty (searching inquiry; require the prosecution to prove guilt; ask if the accused wishes to present evidence) and rebuking counsel de oficio for changing the plea to guilty nine days after a not-guilty plea; and People v. Chua (per Puno), where the searching inquiry, conducted only in English with no determination of the accused's comprehension, failed

The right to counsel as substance, not form: 'an efficient and truly decisive legal assistance and not a simple perfunctory representation'; courts cautioned against sacrificing due process to 'sheer speed' in disposing of capital cases

Justice Vitug's article 'The Death Penalty Sentence -- In Perspective': a mandatory single death penalty unconstitutionally infringes judicial prerogative, drawing on US jurisprudence -- McGautha v. California, Furman v. Georgia (arbitrary, discriminatory imposition violates the Eighth Amendment), and Woodson v. North Carolina and Roberts v. Louisiana (striking down mandatory death statutes for ignoring the individual offender and the particular offense), with Trop v. Dulles grounding the inquiry in 'the dignity of man'

The worldwide abolition trend: about 110 countries supporting a ban (up from fewer than 30 in 1970), a 3.2-million-signature petition to the UN, and Secretary-General Kofi Annan's support for a moratorium

stances.claim: Special qualifying circumstances that raise a penalty to death (such as minority or the offender's relationship to the victim) must be BOTH specifically alleged in the information AND proven at trial; absent either, the death sentence cannot stand and must be reduced to reclusion perpetua -- a doctrine many trial courts kept violating, which is why a 'vast majority' of the Court's death-case decisions imposed lesser penalties. 'More of the same' -- the same safeguard, repeatedly enforced.
stances.rhetorical_move: allege-and-prove safeguard: insisting on a rigid pleading-and-proof rule as a due-process bulwark against erroneous death sentences
stances.confidence: settled doctrine, repeatedly reiterated by the Court

stances.claim: A plea of guilty to a capital offense triggers a mandatory three-step duty under Rule 116, Section 3 -- a 'searching inquiry' into voluntariness and comprehension, requiring the prosecution to prove guilt, and asking whether the accused wishes to present evidence -- and the right to counsel must be 'efficient and truly decisive,' not 'perfunctory'; courts must not sacrifice this to 'sheer speed,' because 'the execution of a death sentence is irrevocable.'
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural-rigor-against-irreversibility: treating strict compliance with plea safeguards as essential precisely because the penalty cannot be undone
stances.confidence: asserted as mandatory doctrine (CJP's own and the Court's)

stances.claim: CJP maintains his philosophical and juridical opposition to the death penalty, and approvingly cites Justice Vitug's view that a mandatory single death penalty unconstitutionally infringes judicial prerogative -- echoing the US Supreme Court's recognition (Furman, Woodson, Roberts) that arbitrary or mandatory capital punishment offends 'the dignity of man' -- against the backdrop of a worldwide abolition trend (about 110 countries).
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-and-trend argument: marshalling US precedent and global abolition data to reinforce a principled objection while conceding the law remains in force
stances.confidence: openly stated as CJP's continuing personal position, presented alongside Vitug's

notable_anecdotes: The empty lethal-injection chamber: CJP records that since President Estrada's March 25, 2000 Jubilee moratorium -- continued by Arroyo's automatic commutations -- no one had been placed in the lethal-injection chamber, even though the Court kept reviewing death sentences because the law had not been repealed.

The Loyola Park shooting: in People v. Gonzales the majority found only homicide where a defenseless pregnant woman, Feliber Andres, was killed by a shot 'not aiming at anybody in particular,' while Pardo's dissent (joined by CJP) saw treachery and aberratio ictus -- the bullet meant for her husband striking her, and shrapnel wounding two children.

Counsel who gave up: in People v. Aranzado and People v. Sta. Teresa the Court chastised defense lawyers who, facing clients who stood to be executed, 'dispensed with the presentation of evidence... notwithstanding the opportunity to present the same' -- the right to counsel meaning real advocacy, 'not a simple perfunctory representation.'

English-only at the gallows' edge: in People v. Chua the searching inquiry was conducted entirely in English with no showing the accused understood it, and his telling remark that 'it is difficult to go against my family' went unexplored -- a failure the Court held denied him due process.

From 30 to 110: CJP notes that the number of countries supporting a ban on executions had grown to about 110 (from fewer than 30 in 1970), with a 3.2-million-signature petition to the UN and Secretary-General Kofi Annan backing a worldwide moratorium.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'A Centenary of Justice' surveys the death-penalty jurisprudence of CJP's sixth year (October 2000-October 2001), its title 'More of the Same' signaling both doctrinal continuity and the persistence of his opposition (developed in 'Battles in the Supreme Court,' 'Leadership by Example' and 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity'). He reports the de facto no-execution policy: President Estrada's Jubilee-Year moratorium (March 25, 2000), continued by the Arroyo government through automatic commutation ('no executions... during [Arroyo's] three-year term'), so no one had entered the lethal-injection chamber since March 2000, even as repeal bills were filed and the Court kept reviewing sentences. The governing safeguard is that special qualifying circumstances under Section 11 of RA 7659 must be BOTH alleged in the information AND proven -- a rule many trial courts violated, so the Court reduced numerous death sentences to reclusion perpetua (for failures to allege a deadly weapon, to independently prove minority, or to establish a qualifying relationship). He catalogues developments including People v. Catubig (exemplary damages on the civil side even when an aggravating circumstance is unalleged) and People v. Gonzales (treachery not lightly inferred from the Loyola Park killing of Feliber Andres -- over a Pardo dissent, joined by CJP, finding treachery and aberratio ictus). A major thread is the improvident-plea line -- People v. Aranzado (per Davide), CJP's own People v. Sta. Teresa, and People v. Chua (per Puno) -- enforcing the mandatory 'searching inquiry' under Rule 116, Section 3 and condemning 'lackadaisical' counsel, since the right to counsel must be 'efficient and truly decisive, not perfunctory' and courts must not sacrifice due process to 'sheer speed' when the penalty 'is irrevocable.' Finally, he approvingly cites Justice Vitug's article that a mandatory single death penalty unconstitutionally infringes judicial prerogative -- marshalling US precedents (Furman, Woodson, Roberts, McGautha, Trop v. Dulles, grounded in 'the dignity of man') -- and closes on the worldwide abolition trend, with about 110 countries now supporting a ban and the UN Secretary-General backing a moratorium.
